I'm designing a hand-crafted policy network for MinAtar Asterix, a 600-32-32-6 MLP with tanh activations. I'm starting by working through the grid layout, where the player sits in rows 1 to 8 of a 10x10 board, and how entities move across those rows at a speed set by move_speed.

I'm working out the safety rules now: an enemy on the player's cell, or one moving onto it, is fatal, while gold adds a point. Since enemies only move horizontally, a row without enemies stays safe until one spawns there, so the player should shift vertically to avoid threats, and I'm weighing whether a 32-unit two-layer network can capture that from the grid channels.

I'm working out how the hidden units can detect a conflict: a unit should fire when the player and an enemy share a row, which is an AND that a single linear layer can't express directly but a tanh threshold can approximate. Since each row holds at most one entity, the player's row indicator and the row's enemy indicator can be summed with a bias so that only the overlap pushes the unit on.

I'm weighing the risk of moving vertically into a row that already has an enemy, versus staying put or heading toward gold in an adjacent row. Enemies move one cell per move_speed frames, so early on I'm faster than they are, but once move_speed drops to 1 we move at the same pace and that margin disappears.

I'm weighing a simple fallback policy: if an enemy shares the player's row, step vertically into a row without one, otherwise head for gold in the same row or an adjacent clear row, and do nothing if neither applies. The catch is that an enemy far off in the same row, moving away, isn't a real threat, so dodging it would be wasted motion, though the cost is small.

I'm checking whether the destination row is safe, which means no enemy there or none close to the player's column, and that would need column-based features. I'm also considering how a single tanh unit can flag a row where the player and an enemy overlap, using a large-gain threshold on the summed indicators to approximate the AND, with one such unit per row.

I'm now weighing whether a column-based feature can separate the gold in the player's own row from gold elsewhere, since a plain sum over all golds mixes rows together. I'm also thinking about how much the score depends on survival versus collecting gold, since trained agents on this game reach only modest scores.

I'm estimating what score a small MLP might reach on Asterix, noting that trained agents usually land in the rough range of 5 to 20. Survival matters most, and the difficulty ramps up over time: spawns speed up toward every frame, and enemies eventually move every frame too.

Now I'm laying out the timing: after about 800 frames the spawn and move speeds bottom out, so every row is almost always occupied and two-thirds of those entities are enemies moving at the player's pace. Next I'll sketch the per-row features I need, namely whether an enemy, gold, or the player sits in each row, along with where the entity is horizontally.

I'm settling on the policy rules now: if an enemy shares the player's row, step up or down into a row without one, preferring the side that's clear. When no enemy is in the player's row, I'll move horizontally toward gold in that row, since the player outpaces enemies early on and can catch gold that drifts away.

I'm considering how to flag a dangerous destination row: an enemy in that row within a column or two of the player. A plain sum can't express that AND across both column positions, and a separate unit for each column would take too many hidden units, so I'm looking for a relative-position encoding instead.

I'm working out a linear feature for the enemy's horizontal offset from the player, which comes out as a sum over columns that's zero when no enemy is in the row. Since that zero gives a misleading value, I'll need to gate the feature on whether the row has an enemy at all, using a tanh threshold to test whether the enemy is within a column or two of the player.

I'm building a unit that fires only when the row has an enemy and that enemy sits at or left of the player's column plus one, using a large offset so the empty-row case stays below the threshold. A mirrored unit would cover the enemy being at or right of the player's column minus one. Combining the two into "within one column" would need a second layer.

I'm considering a more compact encoding that uses coordinates relative to the player's row, instead of spending a separate unit on each row. The catch is that checking the row directly above or below would need a product of the player's row and an enemy's row, which a single linear layer can't express on its own.

I'm stuck on the same problem again: checking "player in row r and enemy in row r-1" needs a product of two row indicators, and doing that for every row takes too many hidden units, so I'm looking for a more compact encoding.

I'm sketching a row-danger unit per row, combining the player's row indicator with that row's enemy indicator, to flag rows that would be unsafe to move into.

I'm trying to get a single tanh unit to detect whether an enemy shares the player's row, since a parity-like test can't be cleanly separated with one linear sum over the row indicators, so I'm considering whether weighting the player and enemy indicators differently could help.

I'm thinking about whether a per-column encoding could work, using relative horizontal positions and row-weighted sums for vertical ones. I'm also weighing a potential-field policy that pushes away from nearby enemies and toward gold, though it would need products of player and entity positions that a linear layer can't express directly.

I'm thinking about a single tanh unit that gates on the player's cell being in a chosen set and fires only when at least one enemy is present, by scaling the weights so the threshold separates those cases.

I'm settling on a single-unit primitive: a tanh unit that fires when the player sits in some chosen set of cells and at least one enemy sits in another chosen set, by making the player's weight large and the enemy weights small with a threshold between them.

I'm trying a different encoding: each unit fires when the player sits in some chosen set of cells and an enemy sits in another, with the weights scaled so the threshold separates the cases. Tying "same row" across rows usually takes a unit per row, so I'm looking at whether a row-index weighting could collapse that into one unit.

I'm building a per-row unit that fires only when the player is in that row and an enemy at or to the right of the player's column is in the same row, by scaling the player's column into the weights so the threshold separates those cases.

I'm checking the per-row unit with a large offset so that when the player is out of the row, the activation stays negative. With both offsets set to 20, the enemy-at-or-left and enemy-at-or-right conditions each separate correctly. That gives 16 units for the two directions across all rows, and the next step would be combining them in a second layer.

I'm thinking about the simpler rule that an enemy in my row means I should move vertically, since every enemy drifts toward the interior and will eventually cross my column. The open question is only which direction to step, up or down.

I'm checking whether the destination row is safe: an enemy one column away from me and approaching would reach my cell on the same frame I step in, so distance one is lethal, and distance two only buys a single move before it closes in.

I'm weighing a safer-row check: whether an adjacent row has an enemy at all, and if both do, which one has its enemy farther from me. Working out a per-row layout for that would take about 32 units, so I'm sketching how the first layer would cover each row.

I'm checking whether a single tanh unit can capture "enemy in an adjacent row near the player's column," which would need a bump in column distance rather than a half-space. A plain additive combination of a function of the player's column and one of the enemy's column can't produce that shape, so I'd need a different encoding for the neighboring-row danger checks.

I'm checking whether one unit can capture "enemy in an adjacent row near the player's column." The distance test would need a bump shape, and that's impossible with additive weights on the player and enemy positions, so I'd need two half-space units combined in a second layer.

I'm checking whether treating any enemy in an adjacent row as blocking would leave me stuck, since enemies are denser later on and most rows would then look unsafe.

I'm weighing a column-based encoding for the adjacent-row danger: one unit per row and side, flagging an enemy in the row above (or below) that sits at or to the left (or right) of the player's column, so the two half-spaces can be combined later.

I'm counting up the units: 16 for each direction across all rows would be too many, so I'm looking for a way to cut the rows that actually matter. I'm considering whether the player could be confined to a small subset of rows, such as rows 1 to 3, which would keep the neighboring-row checks manageable.

I'm settling on the idea of restricting the player to a few rows, which would keep the number of units manageable. Gold appears uniformly across rows, so staying within a small band would cut the score a bit but make survival easier, and survival comes first.

I'm estimating gold income for a two-row policy: spawns run about 0.8 per frame at steady state, roughly 0.27 gold per frame overall, which works out to about 0.067 per frame if I stay in two of the eight rows.

I'm sketching the expected score for this game: a MinAtar-style DQN lands around 15 on Asterix, so an MLP policy near 5 to 15 would be competitive. Next I want to trace the timeline from the start, when spawns happen every 10 frames and entities move every 5, to see how the difficulty ramps up.

I'm working through the timeline now: the ramp fires every 101 frames, with move speed dropping to 1 around ramp 7 and spawn speed reaching 1 at ramp 8, so the game is hardest by about frame 900.

I'm checking the timing rules next: move speed 1 means an entity moves every frame, and move speed 5 means it moves every five frames. The policy will use sharp logits so the chosen action is nearly deterministic despite the 10% sticky-action repeat.

I'm laying out the policy rules: if an enemy shares my row, I step vertically, going up when the row above looks safe and I'm not already on the top row, otherwise down when the row below is safe and I'm not on the bottom row. I'm also noting that at the edges the vertical move would be a no-op, and considering a horizontal fallback since I'm faster than the enemies early on.

I'm still working out the escape rule: if an enemy shares my row, I step vertically, and I only want to enter an adjacent row when no enemy is within a column or two of me there, since at distance two it closes in after one move.

I'm trying to make the adjacent-row check cheaper: instead of conditioning on the player's row, I'd have layer one compute, for each row, two half-space units on the enemy's position relative to the player's column, and combine them later.

I'm settling the encoding for the neighboring-row checks: one shared set of player-column weights works for every row, so each row gets its own pair of half-space units on the enemy's position relative to my column, with a threshold that keeps empty rows silent.

I'm working out how to get the player's row into layer two, either through eight one-hot passthrough units or a single scalar with a tanh threshold, since the scalar would be too coarse to separate rows cleanly.

I'm weighing how to get the player's row into the second layer: eight one-hot passthrough units would take up a lot of the first layer, while a single scalar would be too coarse to isolate one row, and I'm running short on units for the gold features.

I'm running into a budget problem: detecting an enemy in each adjacent row needs one-hot player-row units plus per-row enemy-presence units, and that uses up nearly all 32 first-layer units, leaving no room for the gold features.

I'm noting that an enemy in row r can be detected as the OR of the two half-space units H_r^L and H_r^R, since every enemy sits on one side or the other of my column. That OR can be built in layer two with a tanh threshold, so the row-danger signal doesn't need its own first-layer units.

I'm checking the bias term for the three-way gate: with the player-row unit weighted at 2 and the two half-space units at 1 each, a bias of -1 keeps the sum negative when the player isn't in the row or when neither side fires, and positive when exactly one side fires.

I'm settling on the second-layer units: one danger detector per row for the player's own row, plus up-blocked and down-blocked detectors for each neighboring row, which comes to 22 units in total. Next I need to decide how the output layer combines them so that danger in the current row and blocked neighbors both push the logits the right way.

I'm weighing what to do when both the up and down rows are blocked while an enemy shares my row, since staying put would mean waiting for it to reach me. A horizontal step away from the enemy's side might be the better fallback than a no-op.

I'm now turning to gold: when it sits in my row, I need to know whether it lies to my left or right. Giving each row its own left and right gold detectors would cost 16 first-layer units, which is more than I can spare.

I'm wondering whether gold can be handled without any horizontal logic at all. Gold enters from one edge and slides across its whole row, so if I hold my row, any gold in it will eventually reach my column, which would make an explicit gold-chasing rule unnecessary.

I'm settling on the rule that when there's no danger I just hold still, since gold slides across its row and will reach my column anyway. The one exception I'm weighing is gold sitting in an adjacent row that isn't blocked, where moving over to grab it looks worth it.

I'm weighing whether horizontal chasing is worth it: gold crosses the whole row, so waiting would eventually bring it to my column, but moving toward it could shorten the wait early on, though that horizontal move could also disturb my alignment with enemies in adjacent rows.

I'm checking whether the gold timing works out: at speed 5 a gold crossing takes about 45 frames, and enemy spawns in my row are rare enough that I'd only be forced out about a third of the time. If I do dodge, the gold keeps moving, so I can slip back once the enemy has passed, with the adjacent-row gold rule handling the return.

I'm checking whether an enemy that's still a few columns away would make me leave the gold row again. Entering when the enemy is at distance three or more seems safe at my speed, though sticky actions could make me oscillate in and out of the row, which is wasteful but not dangerous.

I'm working out how to keep the gold-row attraction from making me bounce in and out of rows: it should only pull me toward a row that has no enemy at all, which means I need a per-row gold indicator on top of the presence units, and the first-layer budget is already tight.

I'm considering whether to keep the player in the middle rows so edge-row cases don't need their own units, which would free up budget for the gold-row signal.

I'm considering restricting the player to rows 2 through 7, so that enemies in rows 1 and 8 never matter and the boundary moves are simply ruled out. That would cut the enemy-row units down to six rows and free up budget for the gold signal.

I'm checking whether restricting the player to rows 2 through 7 holds up, since sticky actions could still push them into row 1 or row 8. In that case there's no danger unit for the edge row, so the player would just sit there until something hits them.

I'm adding a fallback for the edge rows: if the player ends up in row 1 or row 8, which sticky actions could cause, there's no danger unit to catch it, so I'll give them a simple push back toward the interior with two extra first-layer units.

I'm checking the layer-one budget now: if I include rows 1 and 8 for danger, I'd need four more units for their H detectors, and that leaves only two spare.

I'm weighing whether to cover all eight rows, which pushes the count to 36 units, four over budget. One option is trimming the gold-direction units for the edge rows.

I'm weighing whether to merge the up-blocked and gold-up signals into one graded unit per row, since the three-way AND over the two side detectors and the gold cell is what's pushing the layer-one budget past its limit.

I'm writing the gold-and-safety unit for each row as a single tanh neuron: it should fire only when the player is in that row, gold sits in the row above, and no enemy blocks the row above.

I'm working out the gold-attraction unit with weights A = B = 2 and a bias of -5, which keeps it positive only when the player is in the row, gold is above, and neither side is blocked. I'm also setting up the blocked-above unit as the conjunction of the player's row and both side detectors.

I'm tallying the layer-two budget again for all eight rows and it comes to 36 units, four over. I'm considering whether to drop some of the danger units or fold them into the gold-attraction units, and I'm sketching what the up and down logits should look like as sums over rows.

I'm checking whether a single threshold unit can capture "player in the row, and either an enemy in this row or gold above, with no block above," since that would save a layer-two unit.

I'm testing whether a single threshold unit can do the whole job: fire only when the player is in the row, an enemy is in the row or gold sits above, and the row above is not fully blocked. Treating the blocked check as a negative weight, the bias has to fall in a narrow window, and I'm checking whether any value of it satisfies both the positive and negative cases.

I'm checking whether one tanh unit can produce the bump for "enemy within two columns of the player," since a single unit would save a layer-one slot. Two half-space units ANDed together is the usual way, but I'm testing whether a clever weighting of the player's and enemy's positions can do it in one.

I'm looking at whether one unit can capture "enemy within two columns of the player," but since an enemy's position added to the player's position only gives a linear split, a single unit can't make the bump. Splitting it into a layer-two conjunction would need a third layer to AND with the row presence, which doesn't fit.

I'm settling on a reduced configuration: keep the danger units for all eight rows but fewer gold-attraction units, using gold attraction upward for rows 3 through 7 and downward for rows 2 through 6, which leaves rows 1 and 8 without a gold pull.

I'm considering dropping the up-block and down-block checks for rows 1 and 8, since the player rarely ends up there, but that feels risky. Another idea is to compute the danger signal for each row directly in the first layer, which would free up second-layer units, though the output still needs a second-layer unit to pass it through.

I'm trying to fold the danger check into the up and down units: an "up OK" unit that fires when the player is in the row, an enemy is in that row, and the row above isn't fully blocked. Whether that conjunction can be a single threshold unit is the open question.

I'm checking the two conditions separately: the enemy-or-trail check is an OR of two half-space units, and the blocked check is an AND of the two side detectors. Combining "enemy present and not fully blocked" into one threshold unit fails too, since the constraints force the bias to be negative and positive at once. So that merged unit won't work, and I'll need a different way to shape the first layer.

I'm looking at whether a layer-one unit can check "player in row r and enemy in row r-1 within two columns," which would take two units per row for each direction and push the total past budget. Adding row-presence units for all eight rows still leaves the count at 36, so the structure has to change.

I'm looking for a way to compress the layer-two budget, since a single graded unit per row could carry the up and down scores as a sum, provided the AND with the player's row saturates cleanly.

I'm trying to make the "up" and "down" scores a single graded unit per row, with the danger check handled by a saturating AND with the player's row. The sum of enemy presence and gold above is only linear in each side, so the OR over the two side detectors doesn't come out cleanly as a threshold.

I'm testing whether a graded sum could give urgency for near versus far enemies, since the enemy-in-row term takes different values depending on distance. The blocked penalty is the trouble, though: an enemy that is far away in the row above would still get penalized, when it should not be.

I'm considering whether the trail cell behind an enemy could stand in for the "blocked" check, since an enemy moving right leaves its trail behind it and the cells ahead are the real danger zone.

I'm wondering whether a single unit can capture "right-moving enemy in this row with the player in its path," since the player cells would need a band of weights that a half-space can't provide, which keeps the check stuck at two units.

I'm checking whether a single unit can encode "enemy within two columns" using the trail channel as well, but any extra cell only adds another function of the enemy's position, so it still stays additive with the player's term and can't form a bump. That means the check needs two units, and I'm reconsidering how to cut the layer-two budget instead.

I'm considering whether the output layer can handle the blocked check on its own: the up logit would sum over per-row danger units, but a blocked penalty from row above would fire regardless of where the player is. Without a conditioning term on the player's row, that penalty leaks into every row, so the output alone can't express it.

Now I'm thinking about trimming the setup: dropping rows 1 and 8 from the blocked checks would save units, but the player might still wander there. Restricting the home area to rows 2 through 7 and handling the edges with a minimal fallback looks like the way to cut the layer-one count.

I'm now tallying the layer-one budget: the row-presence units for rows 1 and 8 can be dropped, since those rows can simply force a move away. That leaves 26 layer-one units with 6 spare, and I'm starting to count the layer-two units needed for the danger and blocked checks in rows 3 through 7.

I'm settling on a layout where rows 1 and 8 get no blocked checks, and I'm adding one danger check for row 1 and one for row 8. I'm also tallying the down-block units for rows 2 through 6, which brings the layer-two count to 13.

I'm tallying the rest of the budget: the gold units for rows 2 through 7 bring the layer-one count to 26, and the output-side checks for rows 1 and 8 would leave 2 spare units.

I'm adding the four row-1 and row-8 horizontal checks and two danger units for those edge rows, which brings layer one to 30 units with 2 spare. Then I'm tallying the layer-two units for all eight rows, starting with the danger and blocked checks.

I'm now trimming the budget further: dropping the up-escape from row 2 and the down-escape from row 7 saves the units I'd need for those edges. That leaves the up checks for rows 3 through 8 and the down checks for rows 1 through 6, which brings the layer-two count to 32.

I'm weighing whether restricting rows 1 and 8 is worth it, since a player in row 2 would lose the up escape while row 1 offers little beyond a return to row 2. I'll keep the rule simple: from row 2 under danger, the player goes down, and if that's blocked, a horizontal escape takes over. I'm also considering letting it go up anyway, but the passthrough would just push it back down.

I'm weighing whether to let the player enter row 1 from row 2 when the down move is blocked, which would make the choice up-or-down come down to a single penalty term. For the bottom edge, I'd give the down logit a small edge in row 1 so it's preferred unless blocked.

I'm settling on the horizontal escape as an "enemy to my right in my row" check: the player's row must hold an enemy with x beyond px+2, which I'd compose from the existing H_r units rather than adding eight new ones, since the layer-one budget is already spent.

I'm weighing whether a horizontal escape is worth the budget, since it only matters when both adjacent rows are blocked and an enemy is already in my row. I'm estimating how often that happens mid-game, roughly half the time my row holds an enemy, so the corner case may come up more than I'd like.

I'm weighing a horizontal escape for the case where both adjacent rows are blocked, but it would cost budget I don't have, and the enemy in my own row usually gives time to wait for the neighbors to clear. I'm leaning toward skipping it, or adding a cheap weak fallback if one fits.

I'm weighing whether a looser blocking band of ±3 columns would be safer, since it would catch enemies that are close enough to clip me during a sidestep, though it would also remove more escape options.

I'm thinking late-game play is a juggling act: with every row occupied, each vertical move has to land on a row whose enemy is still at least three columns away, and that safe window shrinks as enemies approach. So the better plan may be to hold still until an enemy gets to about three columns away, then switch to a row where the nearest enemy is far.

I'm checking whether an enemy in my row is actually approaching, since a unit that fires on any enemy in the row would make me leave even when that enemy is moving away. The trail channel could tell direction, using the cell just behind each enemy to see which way it's heading.

I'm checking whether a trail cell can tell me which way an enemy is moving, since a right-mover approaching from the left would sit at ex - 1 behind it. That would let me blocking-check only the enemies actually closing in, rather than every enemy in the row.

I'm checking whether the trail cell tells me if an enemy is approaching or moving away, by comparing the trail's distance from the player with the enemy's distance. I'm also testing a combined expression to see if it separates the two cases cleanly.

I'm checking whether the trail could tell approaching enemies apart from receding ones, but the sign of the relation flips between right-movers and left-movers, so a single linear unit won't cover both. The gold entities also leave trails, so the trail alone can't separate the two unless each row holds only one kind of entity.

I'm considering whether an enemy that has already passed should still count as danger, since it's moving away and will leave the row on its own. Making the danger check direction-aware would avoid leaving rows unnecessarily, but the trail channel can't separate enemy trails from gold trails cleanly, so the added complexity may not be worth it.

I'm now wondering whether direction-aware danger is worth it: a receding enemy in my row still triggers an escape, which costs extra vertical moves, but the budget would need two units per row to separate approaching from receding, and there isn't room for that.

I'm now making the layer-one horizontal units direction-aware: a right-moving enemy in my row counts as a threat only while it sits at or just past my column, and a left-moving one only while it sits at or just past it from the other side. Together those two units would say whether an enemy in my row is approaching or has just passed. I'm still checking whether the blocking band for entering a row, meaning exactly where a right-mover or a left-mover is close enough to matter, fits inside the budget.

I'm considering a single "threat" unit per row that flags an enemy moving toward me, but a plain blocking check would need a separate half-space for each direction, which doubles the units per row. I'm wondering whether treating any direction-aware threat as blocking could stand in for the full bump check.

I'm considering whether the danger check for a row could go by whether an enemy is approaching, using two direction-aware units per row. Since that would cost more budget than I have, I'm wondering if treating any approaching enemy as blocking, regardless of distance, is a workable stand-in.

I'm defining a unit that fires for a right-moving enemy at or left of my column, meaning it's approaching or sitting on me, and a mirrored one for left-movers. The idea is that an enemy at my exact column counts as blocking when I try to enter that row.

I'm looking at whether a threat unit per row can stand in for the full bump check: a right-mover at or behind my column counts as threatening, and so does a left-mover at or ahead of it. That would give each row a coarse blocked flag, and the upward, downward and move-in conditions would just combine those flags with the row's presence and gold units.

I'm comparing that against the distance-based version, which blocks only within ±2 columns but fires on receding enemies too, and I'm leaning toward the direction-aware approach since it leaves rows with receding enemies usable as escape options. I'm wondering whether to use the distance as well, perhaps by treating an enemy exactly on my column as blocking while strictly-left approachers count as threats.

I'm checking whether a right-moving enemy at or left of my column counts as a threat, using the trail cell just behind it to confirm its direction. That would let me treat any approaching enemy as blocking without needing a distance cutoff.

I'm working out how to tell an enemy's direction from the trail cell beside it: a right-mover at x has its trail at x-1, a left-mover at x+1, and spawns at x=0 or x=9 can be read as right or left by position alone.

I'm now working on the trail encoding: a right-mover at column ex leaves its trail at ex-1, and I want a weight that makes the sum fire only when the enemy is moving right and sits at or left of my column. I'm trying a linear form where the enemy's column and its trail's column each contribute, and checking whether a single threshold can separate the two directions.

I'm checking the constraints on the weights: the right-mover case needs to fire when the enemy is at or left of my column, and the left-mover case must never fire. Setting the margins against each other, the condition at the boundary column reduces to requiring M + K to be at least K·px + θ.

I'm checking whether a single slope on the trail cell can make the threshold work: the right-mover at ex=px must fire, but at ex=px+1 it must not, and the uniform K term breaks that step, so the coefficient on the enemy column has to match the trail's coefficient.

I'm trying to tell an enemy's direction from the trail cell next to it, and the trail needs a weight that depends on its position. A constant trail weight won't separate right-movers from left-movers. I'm testing a weight that scales with column, and working out how the enemy's own weight has to change so the two cancel correctly.

I'm checking the sign conditions for the left-mover case: with the direction term at minus K, its activation falls below zero whenever 2K exceeds px minus ex plus a half, so I'm picking K large enough to keep it silent.

I'm checking the edge case where a right-mover sits at column 0 with no trail cell behind it, and whether the bias term still keeps that row silent.

I'm noticing that a left-mover can also sit at x=0 after moving left from 9, so position alone doesn't settle its direction there, and I'm checking whether the edge bonus at column 0 still separates the two cases.

I'm checking the edge case at column 0, where a right-mover has no trail cell and a left-mover still has one at column 1. Giving column 0 an extra bonus makes the right-mover fire every time, but it also makes a left-mover there fire once the player is far enough away, which is a small false alarm.

I'm checking the edge case at column 0 with a larger K of 10, and confirming that a left-mover there stays silent. For a left-mover at a middle column, the trail term pushes the activation well below zero. The one case still open is a left-mover just spawned at column 9, which has no trail yet and seems to come out strongly positive.

I'm settling on b(9) as a special value that mimics a left-mover's trail, so a newly spawned left-mover at column 9 stays below threshold. I'm also checking the right-mover at column 9, which can't fire anyway since the player would have to be at column 9 as well.

I'm setting the player's column as the same value across every row, and giving enemy cells, trail cells, and the bias the adjusted weights I just worked out, with special values at the edge columns. Then I'm planning to scale the whole thing by a gain of 2 to 4 so the tanh output gets sharp.

I'm checking the right-mover case in general: for an enemy at column ex with its trail at ex-1, the activation simplifies to px - ex + 0.5, so it's positive exactly when the enemy is at or left of the player's column. I'm going to scale layer 1 by a gain of about 4 so the tanh outputs saturate near ±0.96, and then size the layer-2 margins to handle that.

I'm checking the remaining edge cases on the left-mover side, where a left-mover at column 0 still has its trail at column 1 and stays silent for large enough K. A right-mover at column 0 with no trail fires regardless of the player's column, and one at column 9 stays silent because the player would have to be there too.

I'm checking the edge case where a gold cell sits in row r with its trail behind it, and working out what that does to the enemy channel's activation there.

I'm now setting up the mirrored version for left-movers, flipping the coordinates so the player's weight becomes 9 minus its column, with the enemy and trail weights adjusted to match.

I'm now checking whether approaching threats are the right thing to flag for my row, since a left-mover and a right-mover both count as danger as long as they're at or past my column. Leaving early is fine, though I'm wondering whether that's really the case when I want to grab gold.

I'm weighing whether leaving immediately costs anything: the only price is time spent in another row.
